items: UK and Canada renew AI security partnership, expanding standards and evaluation cooperation — importance 5/10 · On 13 October 2026, the UK and Canadian governments announced renewal of their AI security partnership. Their statements prioritize interoperable AI security standards, information sharing on frontier risks and capabilities, regular technical exchanges, and exploration of staff exchanges and coordinated evaluations by the UK AI Security Institute and Canadian AI Safety Institute. The announcement describes intended cooperation; it gives no signed operative text, budget, delivery timetable or evidence that coordinated evaluations have begun. — FCMO-73F9503FD474

ANEEL reports approval of phased rules for sharing renewable generation curtailment in Brazil — importance 5/10 · On 6 October, Brazil’s electricity regulator ANEEL reported that its board approved a rule organizing mandatory generation cuts during renewable-energy oversupply and some electrical constraints. The agency summary says eligible generation cuts will be shared across sources, with hydroelectric generation associated with spillable energy phased in at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% over four years. It also summarizes a boundary for self-producers, a shadow period beginning 180 days after publication and lasting 12 months, and definitive application 18 months after publication. This is the regulator’s announcement of the decision; the signed resolution, publication date and realized cost allocations were not recovered. — FCMO-E338876726B6

EU Commission schedules special scientific-panel meeting on frontier AI risks after reported loss-of-control investigations — importance 5/10 · A European Commission press release dated 9 October 2026 announced a special meeting of the AI Act Scientific Panel on frontier AI safety and security risks. In a Spanish-language follow-up published 12 October, the Commission says the meeting addressed recent loss-of-control incidents, model monitorability and recursive self-improvement; it summarizes four recommendations, including governance of internal-model risks, stronger incident-investigation capacity, international information sharing and scrutiny of training techniques that reduce monitorability. The Commission also says it will send combined questions to developers as it investigates incidents. The sources do not identify the incidents or models, publish the questions, or establish that the recommendations became binding policy. This is a first-party account of advisory work, not independent incident verification. — FCMO-CA575C0CC53D

Anthropic opens a Singapore office and signs an AI safety and adoption MOU — importance 4/10 · Anthropic announced on 14 October that it opened a Singapore office and signed a memorandum of understanding with Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information. The company says the MOU plans technical exchanges on AI safety, security, model evaluation, testing standards and incident response; research on AI adoption and its effects; and support for responsible AI adoption in public and private sectors. CNA independently reports that the MOU was signed on 13 October. The MOU text and implementation results were not located, so the described work remains planned cooperation rather than a demonstrated evaluation or policy outcome. — FCMO-77546960A9C1

Bennet and Welch propose a federal agency with pre-release AI review authority — importance 4/10 · Senators Michael Bennet and Peter Welch announced a proposal for a Federal Digital Commission with oversight powers spanning frontier AI and large digital platforms. Their press release describes proposed pre-certification, a possible pause of certain high-risk model releases, incident-reporting and mitigation duties, and civil penalties up to 15% of prior-year global revenue. This is a proposal described by its sponsors, not an introduced or enacted law; the underlying legislative text was not located in this review. — FCMO-AF98C3034ACF

blocks.text: reasoning_posttraining

items: SkillGym reports agent training gains from executable human-workflow environments — importance 7/10 · A September 2026 preprint introduces SkillGym, a pipeline that turns human-written agent skills into executable tasks with code-based outcome checks and contrastive skill-dependence labels. The authors report 2,756 environments across 12 categories and 8,364 successful trajectories, then fine-tune Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on SkillGym trajectories. They report gains on GDPval-AA v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, including performance that persists without inference-time skills. These remain paper-reported results. The paper’s v2 abstract and v2 HTML disagree on the no-skills SkillsBench gain (12.38 versus 14.68 points), and the reported benchmark comparisons depend on specific harnesses; code, dataset and model artifacts were not audited in this review. — FCMO-13F455C3307C

RLVR rollout batches trade sample efficiency against training stability — importance 6/10 · An arXiv paper reports controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and related checkpoints. Across 21 unclipped runs spanning a 32-fold optimizer-batch range and nearly sixfold learning-rate range, the authors find that training failure timing is more consistent with consumed response samples than optimizer steps along square-root learning-rate scaling. They also report declining sample efficiency above a learning-rate-dependent critical batch, with clipping delaying failure but not removing the progress gap. The results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced. — FCMO-B374C55F976B

Tev reports long-horizon agent training gains from verified environments and dense progress rewards — importance 6/10 · A 13 October preprint introduces Tev-Gym, a 1,170-environment synthetic training corpus with hidden latent-world specifications, strict task verifiers and staged progress scores. The authors use progress-potential reward shaping to train Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B, reporting higher scores than their base checkpoints on Agents’ Last Exam’s computing-and-math subset (ALE-CM). Tev-27B’s reported Pass@5 is 0.28 versus 0.17 for its base and equals the paper’s reported GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 values under the listed harness. The authors also report transfer to selected Terminal-Bench computing-and-math subsets and a larger GLM-5.3-Flash model. These are author-reported results; this review did not independently reproduce them, and the project page lists code and data as forthcoming. — FCMO-93E0233B115D

RECAP uses dependency-aware step credit to reduce reasoning tokens in math models — importance 5/10 · The arXiv preprint introduces RECAP, which gives GRPO training step-level credit using LLM-annotated semantic dependencies plus a gold-answer likelihood signal. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, the authors report 2.0–3.7 percentage-point pass@1 gains and 8–31% fewer reasoning tokens than GRPO across GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024 and AIME 2025. Results on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B are mixed, so the paper does not establish a uniform cross-model improvement. These are author-reported experiments, not independently reproduced; the tested regime is limited to two 7B math models and four benchmarks. — FCMO-CCFA19CB7927

CC-OPD uses counterfactual teacher scores to improve multi-constraint instruction following — importance 5/10 · The CC-OPD preprint proposes assigning token-level training signals to individual instruction constraints by comparing a frozen teacher's scores with and without each constraint. In experiments reported by the authors, CC-OPD had the highest average among the tested methods across seven benchmarks and two Qwen model pairs; a Qwen2.5-1.5B student exceeded its GRPO-IR-trained 7B teacher on MulDimIF. These are preprint-reported outcomes, not independently reproduced results, and the evidence covers only the tested models and training setup. — FCMO-981CF89EA200
